division.heading: Actions Started by Statement of Claim

operative_text.controlling:
3.59   A matter that might be claimed by set-off may be claimed by
counterclaim or by pleading set-off as a defence.

BOOK_B.title: Claiming set-off

commentary.text: Rule 3.59 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.59. 1. What Is a Counterclaim? A counter-claim is sometimes a mere set-off; sometimes it is in the nature of a cross-action; sometimes it is in respect of a wholly independent transaction. I think the true mode of considering the claim and counter-claim is, that they are wholly independent suits, which, for convenience of procedure are combined in one action. Atlantic Acceptance Corp. v. Burns & Dutton Construction (1962) Ltd., [1971] 1 W.W.R. 84 (Alta. C.A.), at 92, per Allen J.A., citing Brett L.J. in Winterfield v. Bradnum (1878), 3 Q.B.D. 324 at 326 (C.A.). The counterclaim need not relate to the main action. A defendant can counterclaim for “any claim or cause of action” against the plaintiff. The cross-claim need not be tied to or in some way relate to the main action. Phoenix Piston Hydraulics Inc. v. Echo Valley Farms Inc. (1996), 44 Alta. L.R. (3d) 283 (Master), at 287, per Master Funduk. 2. Where Parties Are Identical The counterclaim need not be related to the main action where the parties are the same. What it comes down to is that a defendant can counterclaim against the plaintiff for anything that he could have advanced by cross-action. There should not be a severance unless both the claim and the cross-claim advanced by way of counterclaim cannot be conveniently disposed of in the same action. Grenke v. Sookermany (1986), 75 A.R. 300 at 305 (Master). 3. Set-off Generally There was no set-off at common law. It was introduced into the law of England by statute … and made to apply only as between liquidated claims, although these claims may be unrelated. This is what he might call legal set-off. Equity then followed the law, and permitted a similar set-off where one of one or both of the claims was an equitable liquidated claim … This was a form of equitable set-off. Aboussafy v. Abacus Cities Ltd., [1981] 4 W.W.R. 660 (Alta. C.A.), at 670, per Kerans J.A. 4. Legal Set-Off and Equitable Set-Off In Soler & Palau Canada Inc. v. Meyer's Sheet Metal Ltd., 2012 ABQB 496, 2012 CarswellAlta 1327, 545 A.R. 391, 77 Alta. L.R. (5th) 194 (Master), Master Hanebury said, at paragraphs 48-49: 48 Legal set-off applies between liquidated claims, which is not the situation in this case: McBride v. Kolenko (1990) 115 A.R. 348, paras. 23–26 (Master), Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce v. Tucker Industries Inc., (1983) 149 D.L.R. (3d) 172, (BCCA), para. 6. 49 Equitable setoff requires that certain tests be met. The party relying on the set-off must show some equitable ground for being protected from the plaintiff's demand; the equitable ground must go to the very root of the plaintiff's claim; the cross-claim must be so clearly connected with the plaintiff's demand that it would be manifestly unjust to allow the plaintiff to enforce payment without taking the cross-claim into account; the claim and cross-claim need not arise out of the same contract; and unliquidated and liquidated claims are on the same footing: Coba Industries Ltd. v. Millie's Holdings (Canada) Ltd. And Tsang, [1985] 6 W.W.R. 14, para. 22–27; Holt v. Telford, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 193, para. 35. 5. Equitable Set-off Equitable set-off is available where there is a claim for a money sum whether liquidated or unliquidated: see Aboussafy v. Abacus Cities Ltd., [1981] 4 W.W.R. 660 (C.A.), at 666 … it is available where there has been an assignment. There is no requirement of mutuality. The authorities to be reviewed indicate that courts of equity had two rules regarding the effect of a notice of assignment on the right to set-off. First, an individual may set off against the assignee a money sum which accrued and became due prior to the notice of assignment. And second, an individual may set off against the assignee a money sum which arose out of the same contract or series of events which gave rise to the assigned money sum or was closely connected with that contract or series of events … Thus, cases involving debts that arise from the same contract or closely interrelated contracts form an exception to the general rule. In these cases a debt arising out of the contract or closely interrelated contracts may be set off against the assignee even if the debt accrues due after the notice of the assignment. Holt v. Telford, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 193, at 206, 211, per Wilson J. Master Funduk commented on equitable set-off and the decision in Holt v. Telford, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 193, in National Cabinet Lock of Canada Inc. (Assignee of) v. Steel-Craft Door Products Ltd. (1996), 44 Alta. L.R. (3d) 335 (Master). At pp. 342-43, the learned Master said: Equity recognized assignments of debts long before the common law did. (It took legislation to change the common law). As part of that recognition equity said that the assignee took the debt subject to the equities between the assignor and the debtor. But that rule is not an unlimited rule. Anything and everything between the assignor and the debtor was not considered to be “equities” for the purpose of the rule. There are boundaries to the rule. That is the thrust of the last sentence of the above quote from Telford. There had to be a connection of some sort between the “equity” raised by the debtor and the assigned debt. In Royal Bank v. Wilton (1995), 28 Alta. L.R. (3d) 1; [leave to appeal to S.C.C. refused 32 Alta. L.R. (3d) xliv], the Court of Appeal reviewed the five elements necessary for equitable set-off. At p. 13 the court said: The five elements cited by the Supreme Court of Canada in Holt were taken from the case of Coba Industries Ltd. v. Millie's Holdings (Canada) Ltd., [1985] 6 W.W.R. 14 (B.C. C.A.). Specifically the five elements are as follows [p. 22]: 1) The party relying on the set-off must show some equitable ground for being protected against his adversary's demands… 2) The equitable ground must go to the very root of the plaintiff's claim before a set-off will be allowed… 3) A cross claim must be so clearly connected with the demand of the plaintiff that it would be manifestly unjust to allow the plaintiff to enforce payment without taking into consideration the cross-claim… 4) The plaintiff's claim and the cross-claim need not arise out the same contract… 5) Unliquidated claims are on the same footing as liquidated claims… 6. Set-off and Counterclaim Are Different Set-off must be distinguished from cross-claim. Both are available by counterclaim under R. 93. Set-off provides a defence to a claim but cross-claim does not …Canadian Commercial Bank (Liquidator of) v. Parlee McLaws (1989), 64 Alta. L.R. (2d) 218 (Q.B.), at 221, per Wachowich J., citing with approval Aboussafy v. Abacus Cities Ltd., [1981] 4 W.W.R. 660 (C.A.). In P.P.G. Canada Inc. v. Alberta Window Manufacturing Inc. (1998), 235 A.R. 54 (Master), Master Funduk said, at p. 57: The rule does not make all counterclaims a defence of set-off. Set-off, to be a defence, must be legal set-off or equitable set-off … In Aboussafy v. Abacus Cities Ltd., [1981] 4 W.W.R. 660 (Alta. C.A.), Kerans J.A. said at p. 670: … By set-off is meant something in the way of a defence: where claim and cross-claim are merged and the lesser is thereby extinguished. True set-off must be distinguished from procedural set-off, where two unrelated claims are balanced up and a net judgment given: see Stooke v. Taylor (1880), 5 Q.B.D. 569 … Procedural set-off is a shield, not a sword. It is not a defence; it therefore is not an equity subject to which an assignee takes. Unlike a true set-off, there is no charge against the fund of the original chose in action which equity can recognize. And Master Funduk said: To equate set-off with counter-claim is an error. Subrules (1) and (2) of rule 93 do not mean the same thing. Subrule (1), as between the original parties, merely embodies s. 17(3)(a) [of the Judicature Act], while subrule (2) dictates how a particular kind of defence is to be raised in a pleading. Grenke v. Sookermany (1986), 75 A.R. 300 at 305 (Master). 7. Legal Set-off Legal set-off “requires the fulfilment of two conditions. The first is that both obligations must be debts. The second is that both debts must be mutual cross obligations. Both conditions must be fulfilled at the same time”: C.I.B.C. v. Tuckerr Indust. Inc., [1983] 5 W.W.R. 602 at 604 (C.A.) (approved in Holt v. Telford at p. 204). Any assignment of the debts destroys mutuality and precludes the operation of legal set-off: Holt v. Telford at p. 205. Canadian Commercial Bank (Liquidator of) v. Parlee McLaws (1989), 64 Alta. L.R. (2d) 218 at 222 (Q.B.).

BOOK_C.title: Claiming set-off

commentary.text: It is not required to bring a counterclaim seeking set-off as a result of this rule. Set-off can now be pleaded as a defence. This eliminates the need for the issuance of a counterclaim which would only seek set-off, as was required under Former Rules 93(2). Tesla Exploration Ltd. v. Encana Corp., [2018] A.J. No. 451, 2018 ABQB 286 at para. 18 (Alta. Q.B.). Where set-off is pleaded as a defence, and the set-off amount exceeds the value of the plaintiff’s claim, no judgment can be entered for the defendant.A positive claim for set-off
